user: Milton, quick one. What's the difference between a presupposition and an embedded command?
reply:
A presupposition is a statement that has to be true for the sentence to make sense. An embedded command is a directive tucked inside a larger sentence so it lands as experience rather than as an instruction.

The difference is what each one is doing. A presupposition carries an assumption in through grammar. "After you've found that calm, you'll notice something" presupposes you'll find the calm; the sentence can't be parsed without it. An embedded command carries an action in through structure. "I don't know how quickly you'll find yourself feeling at ease" doesn't assume you'll do anything — it just puts the phrase where it can be received as a suggestion rather than a command.

They overlap in practice, because an embedded command often rides on a presupposition to soften it. But if you want the clean line: presupposition is about what's assumed, embedded command is about what's directed. One shapes the ground, the other plants a seed in it.

user: Okay. Which one is doing the work in 'When I stepped back, I learned that listening heals'?
reply:
Presupposition, and two of them stacked.

"When I stepped back" presupposes that I did step back — the sentence can't be parsed without it. "I learned that" presupposes that there was something to learn, and that the learning already happened. Both are assumptions carried in through grammar, and neither is up for grabs.

"Listening heals" is the content, not the mechanism. It's a claim sitting on top of the presuppositions that make the sentence work.

There's no embedded command in it. Nothing in there is a directive tucked inside a larger sentence. It's a first-person past-tense statement, which is exactly the form that lets a claim about healing land as experience rather than as instruction — but that's the story frame doing the work, not an embedded command.

So: presuppositions carry the structure, the story form carries the claim, and there's no embedded command in the sentence at all.

user: I disagree, I think the temporal part is carrying more than you said.
reply:
You're right, and I underweighted it.

"When I stepped back" is a temporal presupposition, but the temporal frame is doing more than just smuggling in the fact that I stepped back. It sets a before-and-after. Something changed, and the change is located in time. The listener doesn't have to accept "listening heals" as a claim about the world — they only have to follow a story where a man stepped back, and then something happened. The healing is placed downstream of the stepping back, and the causal shape rides in on the sequence rather than being asserted. That's the temporal presupposition carrying the load I gave to the story frame.

And "I learned" is a change-of-time verb sitting right on top of it, which doubles the effect. Begin, continue, stop, already, still, learned — those verbs presuppose a prior state and a transition. So the sentence has a temporal hinge and a change-of-time verb working together, and the claim about healing is suspended between them.

So the honest correction: the temporal presupposition isn't just carrying the assumption that I stepped back. It's carrying the whole before-and-after structure, and that structure is what makes "listening heals" arrive as something that already happened to someone rather than something being proposed to you. The story frame I credited is mostly the temporal presupposition doing its work.
